title: Round 1: Explain your architecture for a production .NET + React application
description: Learn to clearly explain a full-stack production architecture using .NET and React. This mock interview round focuses on structuring your answer from the frontend through the API, database, and deployment pipeline.

data.text: In the first round, the interviewer asks you to walk through the architecture of a production application built with .NET on the backend and React on the frontend. The goal is not to describe a single perfect diagram, but to show that you understand how the pieces fit together, where the boundaries are, and how the system behaves under real-world traffic.

Start with the user's browser. The React app is served as static assets from a CDN or from an ASP.NET Core app that also hosts the API. When the user logs in, the frontend sends credentials to the backend, which validates them and returns a JWT or session cookie. From that point on, every API request carries that identity.

items: Frontend: React app with code splitting, lazy-loaded routes, and a state-management strategy
API layer: ASP.NET Core Web API with controllers or minimal endpoints, validation, and authorization filters
Domain layer: C# classes and interfaces that hold business rules independent of the web framework
Data access: Entity Framework Core repositories or a lightweight data-access layer
Database: Relational database with migrations, connection pooling, and read replicas if needed
Caching: In-memory or Redis cache for frequently accessed data with an invalidation strategy
Background jobs: Hosted services or a queue for long-running work such as sending emails

data.text: A strong answer connects these components with actual data flows. For example, when a user submits a form, the React component calls an API endpoint, the endpoint validates the model, the domain service enforces a business rule, the repository saves the change, and the frontend updates the cache.

items: Authentication and authorization: Where tokens are validated and how roles are enforced
Error handling: Global exception handling, problem-details responses, and client-friendly messages
Logging and monitoring: Structured logging, correlation IDs, and health checks
Deployment: CI/CD pipeline, environment variables, containerization, and blue-green or rolling updates
Testing: Unit tests for domain logic, integration tests for API endpoints, and end-to-end tests for critical paths

data.title: Interview tip
data.text: Draw a quick diagram if you are in a whiteboard or virtual interview. Label the client, API, database, cache, and background worker. Then narrate a single user request through the diagram. Interviewers reward clarity over completeness.

If you have time, mention trade-offs. For instance, a monolith with clean architecture boundaries is easier to deploy than a microservice architecture for a small team. Separating the frontend and backend into different repositories improves autonomy but adds deployment complexity.

data.title: Summary
points: Explain the full stack from user to database
Name the key components and their responsibilities
data.takeaway: Keep the narrative simple and grounded in production concerns like logging, caching, and deployment.
